They also enjoy short picture book biographies and accessible poems corresponding to the historical time period as relevant, and lesson plans occasionally point out interesting poetic features.

blocks.text: Poetry reading should be brief and pleasurable. There are also many lovely picture books of poems to include as free reads at this age (see Extra Helpings). Remember that poems are like paintings--they not only convey ideas, they create an experience with the sound of words, the way the words are arranged, and the emotions, thoughts, and images they evoke.

Read the poem aloud a time or two. As students gain reading fluency, let them read the poem as well. It is helpful to hear poetry read by different voices. Try to read paying attention to the punctuation as well as the line breaks to get the sense of the poem.

Allow students to share any thoughts or connections. What are your impressions of the poem? Talk about anything that stood out to you: the images, ideas, words, phrases, sounds, or even physical look of the poem. What kinds of things is the poem about?
Read the poem aloud again. Poetry is meant to be savored like a chocolate that you roll around in your mouth until the last bit melts.

lessons.title: 5m Poetry: Grades 1-4 - Lesson 1
lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Over the River and Through the Woods

➜ NOTE
You will usually spend one week reading the poems from around 5 pages of the book (depending on the size of the illustrations and length of poems). You can pick 1-3 to read each day and reread them as much as you like. Poetry is made to be read many times. Lessons give some ideas for discussing a particular poem, but those are only suggestions. You'll also focus particularly on getting to know the poet Rabindranath Tagore in Term 1, Effie Lee Newsom in Term 2, and Emma Lazarus in Term 3. Feel free to use the index of the book to look up other poems by poets you particularly like.

➜ INTRO 
Almost all the poems we'll read this year were written from 1800 to 1900 AD (the time period you'll learn about in many of your other lessons as well). So, as you read, imagine children like you listening to these same poems about 200 years ago! First, let's start by reading a poem about poetry.

lessons.title: 5m Poetry: Grades 1-4 - Lesson 2
lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Over the River and Through the Woods

➜ INTRO
Our poem today is by Paul Lawrence Dunbar. He was one of the first Black Americans to earn a living as a writer, and he inspired many other writers after him. He also became friends with Orville Wright and his brother Wilbur (who you may remember as the inventors of the airplane)! The Wright brothers owned a printing press and published Dunbar's first writings. 

➜ READ & DISCUSS
p.36 "The Seedling" by Paul Lawrence Dunbar

• Do you notice how the seedling starts talking in the poem? Have you ever heard a seedling talk? Of course not! Poets sometimes imagine that things like plants or animals can talk to help us think about them in new ways. The fancy word for this is "personification." Do you notice any other examples of the seed doing things only people normally do?
lessons.teacherNotes:
★ TEACHER NOTE
Optional: This glossary from the Poetry Foundation may be useful for teachers, though terms will be described in the lesson plans. 
∞ Link: Glossary of Poetic Terms 

Personification is sometimes confused with anthropomorphism, which is when animals or objects actually behave like humans. (Think of Peter Rabbit walking on two legs and wearing clothing as an example of anthropomorphism.)

lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Crescent Moon

➜ INTRO 
Rabindranath Tagore was born in 1861 in Calcutta, India, and grew up in a family that loved art, music, and ideas. He was a poet, short-story writer, composer, playwright, and painter who spent his life creating in many different ways. In 1913, he became the first non-European writer to be awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature. He also composed the national anthems for both India and Bangladesh, making his words a lasting part of two nations. Once a week this term, we'll explore poems by Rabindranath Tagore exploring themes like mothers, children, and nature. 

➜ READ & DISCUSS
p.8 "On the Seashore" 

• What are the children doing at the seashore?

lessons.title: 5m Poetry: Grades 1-4 - Lesson 6
lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Over the River and Through the Woods

➜ READ & DISCUSS
p.50  "In Blossom Time" by Ina Coolbrith

• Notice that each verse has exactly four lines. Poems often have many different types of hidden structure to make the words sing. Another type of pattern in the poem is rhyme. Notice how the last words in the 2nd and 4th lines of each verse sound similar. Can you come up with some rhyming words?

lessons.title: 5m Poetry: Grades 1-4 - Lesson 7
lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Over the River and Through the Woods

➜ READ & DISCUSS
p.44 "Prairie Fires" by Eudora May Stone and p.46 "The Mushroom's Soliloquy" by Hannah Flagg Gould

• Keep an eye out for hidden patterns in poems. Do they have a set number of lines for each verse? Can you hear or see any rhymes?
• A soliloquy is when a character speaks their private thoughts or feelings out loud without anyone else around to hear them. What are some of the mushroom's thoughts?
lessons.teacherNotes:
★ TEACHER NOTE
"Prairie Fires" on page 44 is a good example of a quatrain (4 lines per stanza) with an ABAB rhyme scheme. (Students can simply point out which words rhyme. Specific rhyme schemes will be taught in later grades.) 
 
"The Mushroom's Soliloquy" on page 46 is also a good example of a quatrain and has an AABB rhyme scheme.

"The Johnny Cake" on page 45 has three lines per stanza, which is called a tercet. The rhyme scheme is ABB. The pace of a tercet is often slower than a couplet or quatrain.

lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Over the River and Through the Woods

➜ INTRO 
John Greenleaf Whittier is known as a passionate abolitionist opposing slavery long before the Civil War, a prolific writer, and a friend to several other famous writers. During his lifetime, he became one of America's most popular poets. He also ran for Congress twice and remained involved in politics throughout his life. He spent his later years writing about religion, nature, and country life. He moved in a remarkable circle of friends that included abolitionist Frederick Douglass, poets Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, and novelist Mark Twain. 

➜ READ & DISCUSS
p.73 "The Barefoot Boy" by John Greenleaf Whittier

• Can you hear the rhymes in Whittier's poem?

lessons.title: 5m Poetry: Grades 1-4 - Lesson 21
lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Over the River and Through the Woods

➜ INTRO 
Louisa May Alcott grew up in Concord, Massachusetts. Her family was neighbors and friends with several famous writers and poets, all of whom influenced her love of writing from an early age. She wrote novels, short stories, and poetry that often drew on her own life and the social causes she cared about. Her poetry also often reflected a love of nature, finding meaning and beauty in the natural world.

➜ READ & DISCUSS
p.83 "Morning Song of the Bees" by Louisa May Alcott

• You'll read a book called "Little Women" by Louisa May Alcott when you're older!
lessons.teacherNotes:
• EXTRA HELPING
∞ Article Link: Louisa May Alcott bio

★ TEACHER NOTE
LMA uses an ABCB rhyme scheme in the first 8 lines, but then changes to an AABCCB scheme in the refrain (the last 6 lines). This creates a "bouncing" effect much like bees bouncing from flower to flower. The poem almost sounds like a song or hymn when read aloud.

lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Over the River and Through the Woods

➜ INTRO 
Helen Hunt Jackson experienced many hardships in her life. She turned to writing to help her through her grief and went on to publish poetry, children's books, and travel writing. She also happened to grow up as a close friend of poet Emily Dickinson! Later in life, Jackson became a fierce champion for Native American rights, writing a book called A Century of Dishonor (1881) after hearing a moving speech by Chief Standing Bear and then writing a novel called Ramona (1884) that told the story of California's displaced Mission Indians. 

➜ READ & DISCUSS
p.103 "The Shining Little House" by Helen Hunt Jackson.

• What do you think the lesson of "The Shining Little House" is? Do you agree?

lessons.title: 5m Poetry: Grades 1-4 - Lesson 31
lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Over the River and Through the Woods

➜ INTRO 
Emily Dickinson spent almost her whole life in Amherst, Massachusetts, rarely leaving her family home. She was a serious gardener who grew all kinds of flowers and plants, and you can see her love of nature in her poems, which are full of flowers, bees, and changing seasons that she observed right in her own backyard. Even though she only published a small handful of poems while she was alive, she secretly wrote nearly 1,800 of them, and most weren't discovered until after she died in 1886. Today, she's considered one of the greatest American poets. Imagine her going back and forth between her garden and her writing desk, getting inspired by everything she saw growing around her.

➜ READ & DISCUSS
p.125 "In the Garden" by Emily Dickinson

lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Over the River and Through the Woods

➜ INTRO 
American poet Laura E. Richards had pretty impressive parents! Her mother was Julia Ward Howe, who wrote "Battle Hymn of the Republic," and her father ran the Perkins Institution for the Blind. She followed in her family's accomplished footsteps by writing nearly a hundred books, becoming a pioneer of nonsense poetry for kids, and even having one of her stories turned into a movie. She and her sister won the Pulitzer Prize for Biography for a book they wrote about their famous mother, making them the first women ever to win that award. 

➜ READ & DISCUSS
p.134 "The Sad Story of the Dandy Cat" by Laura Richards

• A dandy is a man who cares too much about appearances and fashion.

➜ INTRO 
Ella Wheeler Wilcox grew up on a farm in Wisconsin, started writing poetry around age eight, and was widely published in magazines by the time she was a teen! She became one of the most widely read American poets of her era. She wrote nearly 40 books of poetry and prose, including the famous lines "Laugh, and the world laughs with you; weep, and you weep alone," which she wrote after comforting a grieving widow on a train. She was also a passionate advocate for animal rights, and this topic came up in several of her poems, like "The Hen's Complaint." 

➜ READ & DISCUSS

Ralph Waldo Emerson was a Boston-born writer, poet, and philosopher who became one of the most influential thinkers in American history. He was unusually curious about Eastern cultures for his time, and he wove ideas from Hindu, Persian, and Chinese texts into his writing. He had some of the cultural blind spots common to people of his era, but he genuinely broadened the horizons of American readers by introducing them to ideas and traditions from around the world.

lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Over the River and Through the Woods

➜ INTRO
Clement Clarke Moore was born in 1779 in New York City and became a college professor of ancient languages. On Christmas Eve 1822, he reportedly wrote a fun poem just to entertain his kids. That poem, "Account Of A Visit from St. Nicholas," was the first to give Santa's reindeer their names and went on to become one of the most beloved Christmas poems ever. It was published anonymously in a New York newspaper in 1823, and Moore didn't claim authorship until 1844. However, the family of another writer, Henry Livingston Jr., argued that he was the real author! Computer analysis in the early 2000s even suggested the poem had more in common with Livingston's known writing style than Moore's. So, the mystery of who really wrote "'Twas the Night Before Christmas" may never be fully solved! 

➜ READ & DISCUSS

lessons.body:
⍞ Materials: Over the River and Through the Woods

➜ INTRO
James Russell Lowell was born in 1819 in Cambridge, Massachusetts. He graduated from Harvard but was banned from the graduation ceremonies for breaking the rules! During his suspension, he stayed with a reverend in Concord, where he met poets Ralph Waldo Emerson and Henry David Thoreau, though his relationship with Thoreau would later sour. He skipped a career in law to pursue writing instead. His wife Maria strongly opposed slavery and pushed him toward more active involvement in the abolitionist cause. The couple gave their own money to help people escaping enslavement, even when times were tough financially. In 1849, he contributed toward purchasing a slave's freedom, writing, "if my poems were more popular, my gifts should be larger." Lowell also joined the Boston Vigilance Committee, a group that provided shelter, clothing, money, and safe passage to slaves seeking freedom on the Underground Railroad. Lowell became the first editor of the Atlantic Monthly and even served as U.S. ambassador to Spain and Great Britain. 

➜ READ & DISCUSS
p.408 "The Fatherland" by James Russell Lowell

• Fatherland means the country, nation, or land you came from. For example, Irish immigrants to America in the 1800s would call Ireland their fatherland.

lessons.teacherNotes:
★ TEACHER NOTE
Some people in the Victorian Era thought poverty was due to a moral failing and that the poor were less intelligent (or less able to learn). They may have also been concerned about the diseases that sometimes spread when poor families often had to live in small apartments (sometimes several families to an apartment) without running water or convenient ways to keep clean. 

If your students are familiar with Charlotte Mason, you can share that she lived in this same time period. She felt strongly that all children were equally capable of learning and deserved a good education.

➜ INTRO
Oliver Wendell Holmes was born in Cambridge, Massachusetts. He became a professor of anatomy at Harvard Medical School and was eventually made its dean, a position he held until 1882. He was also one of the "Fireside Poets," beloved for writing poetry that families could enjoy together. His most famous poem, "Old Ironsides," helped save the historic warship USS Constitution from being scrapped by the Navy. His son was Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., who became an Associate Justice of the Supreme Court of the United States. Holmes Jr. graduated from Harvard in 1861, right as the Civil War was breaking out, and enlisted in the Union Army. He was wounded three times, and his father wrote a famous essay about frantically searching for his son after the Battle of Antietam. 

➜ READ & DISCUSS
p.413-417 "Grandmother's Story of Bunker-Hill Battle: As She Saw It From the Bellfry" by Oliver Wendell Holmes.  

• This poem was written for the centennial (100th) anniversary of this Revolutionary War battle. Watch for an interesting twist at the end of the poem regarding the legacy of an injured soldier.
